dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: Is it my turn yet? How much longer is this going to take? Am I going to miss the train?

dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: Huh? You recognize me? Are you one of my readers? Wow, I didn't realize I was getting so famous...

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: Looks like you'll be waiting for a while more.

dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: Yeah, looks like it. There was a young couple arguing here earlier — they were really going at it. The attendants didn't even lift a finger... Though I suppose there wasn't much they could do.

dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: After that, the two of them just walked off in opposite directions. The child still here must be theirs. The poor thing must have a difficult home life.

dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: Still, if the ticket clerk takes any longer with him, I'm going to be the one in trouble. Standing in line for long just to miss my train... That'd be so infuriating.

dialogues.speaker: Player
dialogues.text: I'll leave you to it, then.

dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: Your train's here already? Well, safe travels.

dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: A reader of "Pioneers," naturally... Ah. Except the paper has never once printed my picture, has it? Right... My mistake. I appear to have promoted myself a little too soon.

dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: Truth be told, I write a little column for "Pioneers." My editor says it's been rather popular with readers lately, and, well, I got carried away and thought fame had finally found me.

dialogues.speaker: Mamontov
dialogues.text: You know, I don't really get it. My serious train features, the ones I research and fact-check properly, keep getting rejected. Meanwhile, the half-true little train anecdotes I write off the cuff turn out to be the hit.
